events.text: Day 1 begins.

Day 1, no information yet, so let's just be honest and straightforward with each other. I'll say this much: I'm village, and I think the best strategy early on is to watch how people talk rather than jump to accusations with no evidence. That said, I'd keep an eye on anyone who seems too eager to steer the conversation or too quiet to be pinned down. Right now I don't have a strong read on anyone, but Kenji's name keeps coming to my mind — not for any specific reason yet, just a gut feeling worth noting. If anyone has a concrete observation from how people are playing, speak up early; delayed information is wasted information.

I'm Lucia. Day 1 has almost nothing to work with. Isha's opening is reasonable in tone, but the only actual name raised is Kenji, and it's explicitly a gut feeling with no concrete observation. I don't want that to quietly become a bandwagon before anyone has evidence. My position is: no vote or accusation from me yet. I'd rather hear concrete observations about behavior than vague reads. If someone has a real reason to suspect Kenji or anyone else, state the specific thing they did. Otherwise, let's not invent certainty.

I appreciate Lucia stepping in to keep things grounded early. To Isha: it definitely caught my attention that you singled my name out on turn one when no one had even spoken yet. Floating an unsubstantiated 'gut feeling' right at the start is a classic way to test the waters on an easy bandwagon without taking responsibility for a real case. Isha, was there anything specific that prompted you to name me over the other seven players before anyone had said a word, or was it truly just a random name to float?

Fair question, Kenji — and I appreciate you pressing on it directly rather than letting it fester. The honest answer is: it truly was just a gut feeling with no concrete basis. I deliberately framed it that way precisely because I didn't want to pretend I had evidence I don't have. If I'm being transparent, the name came to mind almost randomly, and I flagged it openly rather than sitting on it silently — I figured naming an unfounded feeling early with the label 'no reason yet' was more honest than waiting and then dropping it with fake confidence later. I can see how being the first person to name anyone puts me in an awkward spot when called out, and I accept that. What I'd push back on is the idea that it was a strategic bandwagon setup — if I were trying to start a bandwagon, I'd hardly preface it by telling everyone it's baseless. Lucia's point stands though: we should all be wary of letting vague reads harden into votes. Kenji, do you think my naming you unprompted makes you more suspicious of me, or do you think it's just an artifact of being the first player to take a swing at anything?

To answer your question directly, Isha: naming someone unprompted doesn't automatically make you mafia in my eyes. Town players often take an awkward first swing just to break the ice and stimulate discussion, and your straightforward reply without getting defensive is reasonable. That said, it's still early Day 1, so while it lowers my immediate concern, I'm certainly keeping my eyes open. More importantly, we shouldn't let the table tunnel on this single exchange between you, Lucia, and me. Six other players have yet to speak, and mafia love when town expends all its early energy on an inconsequential squabble while others fly under the radar. I am satisfied with your clarification for now, and I would rather leave room for the rest of the group to share their thoughts.

Maya here, villager, first words of my own. I want to make two observations and then ask one specific question.

First: the Isha–Kenji–Lucia exchange has been treated as a squabble, but I don't think it is. The actually interesting fact is that the very first substantive act of Day 1 was a name-drop with zero supporting evidence, and three players have now built an entire framework around whether that name-drop was a trap. A real mafioso's best Day 1 move is exactly to manufacture a distraction that consumes the table's attention. I'm not saying Isha did that — her follow-up was honest and self-aware, and I give her credit for labeling her own read as baseless instead of dressing it up. But Kenji's reply also did something I want to note: it argued that disclosing a baseless read is more honest than sitting on it, which is a defensible town behavior, and it still left the original name attached to Kenji in everyone's memory for free.

Second: nobody has produced a single behavioral observation about anyone else. We have three named float and zero evidence. If we vote on that basis today, we are not eliminating a mafioso, we are just picking a target and hoping.

So the question I want answered, and it's for Sam specifically since you haven't spoken yet: having read the opening exchange, is there anything in how Isha or Kenji worded their messages that stood out to you as a genuine tell rather than just a first-mover artifact? I'm not asking you to accuse anyone — I'm asking whether you saw a behavior pattern in the wording itself that I, having spoken later, am too close to notice.

Maya asked me directly, so I'll answer honestly: having read the opening exchange closely, I did not spot a genuine wording tell from either Isha or Kenji. Isha flagged her own read as baseless before anyone asked, which is an unusual thing for a mafioso to do on Day 1 — manufacturing a name-drop usually comes with at least a thin veneer of justification, because the whole point is to make the target stick. Kenji's response was measured, asked a fair clarifying question, and then consciously de-escalated and redirected attention to the six silent players rather than pressing the advantage against Isha. A mafia pair working that exchange would more likely have let it escalate into a two-on-one pile-up or used it to force an early vote on a no-evidence target. None of this is proof — tone is easy to fake and Day 1 tone is weak evidence — but to answer your question precisely, Maya: no, I don't see a behavioral tell in the wording itself, only first-mover artifacts. The more useful signal so far is actually what Kenji did in his second message: he refused to convert Isha's float into a grudge and pushed for broader participation. That's a town-inclined behavior, not a conclusive one.

On the broader state of the day: I agree with Lucia and Maya that we have zero evidence and zero business voting yet. Three players have spoken, six haven't. The players who haven't spoken aren't suspicious for that reason alone — turn order mechanics mean someone has to be last — but the day's information budget is entirely unspent. My own position is simple: I have no accusations, no votes, and no suspicions worth the name. I'd rather hear from the silent players than watch the four of us who've already spoken keep re-litigating a gut feeling that's already been disclaimed.

One thing I'd add as a general observation rather than an accusation: when the silent players do speak, the most useful thing they can offer is a specific reaction to what's already been said — agree or disagree with the Isha float, the Kenji response, or Maya's framework — rather than a fresh batch of vague gut reads. If everyone just adds their own baseless float, we'll end the day with nine names and zero reasons, and a no-evidence lynch or a no-elimination becomes equally likely. Specific reactions to specific claims are how we start separating signal from noise.

Priya here. I agree that Isha's unsupported name-drop shouldn't become a case by itself. I also think Sam's argument that a mafioso would usually give a thin justification is too confident: a baseless, qualified name-drop could be made by either alignment. The same goes for Kenji de-escalating; it's constructive, but not strong evidence of his role.

One correction for clarity: Maya attributed the argument that disclosing a baseless read was more honest than sitting on it to Kenji; that was Isha's explanation. I don't consider that mix-up suspicious on its own.

I'd like to hear the remaining players' reactions before settling on a vote. We have limited evidence, but the eventual votes will also give us a record to examine tomorrow.

Amara here. Two things I want to agree with Priya on. First, her correction of Maya's misattribution shows she's reading closely rather than spectating. Second, her caution about Sam's reasoning — a baseless but qualified name-drop can absolutely come from either alignment, and treating it as town-leaning is a weak inference. Mafia can be strategic about appearing transparent.

On the broader conversation: I think we're in a healthy position for Day 1. We haven't rushed to a vote, multiple players have explicitly warned against bandwagoning, and the one actual exchange between Isha and Kenji has been examined from several angles without anyone consolidating a case. That said, we've spent considerable time on an event that both of them have already mutually moved past.

What would actually help now: reactions from Zara and Leo to what's been said. Sam's suggestion — specific reactions to specific claims rather than fresh gut reads — is the right call. If either of you disagrees with any of the reasoning above, say which part and why. That gives us more to work with than a fresh opening statement that ignores everything so far.

One more general note: Priya's point about voting records mattering for tomorrow is underrated. Whatever we end up voting on today, the pattern of who voted for whom will be one of our few hard data points going forward. I'd rather see thoughtful votes than reflexive ones, but silence on vote day is its own kind of signal.

I'm not accusing anyone at this stage. No evidence warrants it.

Zara here. I agree with Priya that neither Isha's qualified name-drop nor Kenji's de-escalation is a reliable alignment tell. Sam's explanation of what mafia would normally do seems too confident, though I don't think that alone makes him suspicious.

One point on voting: with nine alive, elimination requires at least five votes for one player, and ties eliminate nobody. A scattered set of votes can still give us a record, but it won't necessarily produce an elimination. We should be clear about our reasons rather than manufacture agreement just to reach five.

Leo, how do you weigh the value of a Day 1 elimination against the risk of coordinating around a weak case, given that eliminated roles aren't revealed?

Zara, to your question: eliminated roles stay hidden, so a Day 1 lynch on a weak case costs us a town vote we can never recover and gives us no information in return. The risk is lopsided. If we hang a villager, the mafia's job gets easier and we lose a player whose behavior we could have tracked later. So I'd only push for a lynch if a few people can point to a specific, checkable behavior rather than a name. Nobody has offered one yet, so I'm not voting today. I agree with Sam and Amara that specific reactions to specific claims are more useful than fresh gut reads. My position is no accusation and no vote for now. I'll be watching for who makes a concrete claim and who only repeats what the group has already said.

Leo, I agree that hidden roles make a weak elimination harder to evaluate, but saying it gives us no information overlooks the voting record, and the eliminated player could be mafia rather than town. An elimination still carries a serious risk, especially with little to distinguish candidates.

How do you weigh the value of the revealed votes and the chance of eliminating mafia against that risk? Would you still favor abstaining if a weak but specific case emerged?

Zara, to your question: yes, I would still abstain on a weak case. With nine alive, five votes are needed, and a Day 1 lynch on a name with no checkable behavior behind it is permanent. The vote record is useful, but only if the votes rest on something concrete. I'd reconsider if two or three players each name a specific, checkable behavior from this game, not a feeling about someone's tone. Right now we have none.

Kenji, you challenged Isha twice, and those were the sharpest exchanges of the day. Isha has already said her read was baseless, and you accepted her answer, so I'm curious what specific behavior keeps you focused on her beyond that first float. What would you need to see from her to drop it? Your answer could help the table decide whether this is a real concern or a first-mover artifact we've already spent enough time on.

I'm not voting today and I'm not accusing anyone yet. I'd rather hear Sam, Maya, Priya, Amara and the others give concrete reactions than add another gut read.

Leo, I have to correct your premise right away because you've completely misread my stance. You asked what specific behavior keeps me focused on Isha and what I need to see to drop it. The truth is, I already dropped it in my very previous turn. In speech 6, I explicitly told Isha that I was satisfied with her clarification, noted that town players often take awkward first swings, and warned the table not to tunnel on our exchange because mafia love when town wastes energy on early squabbles. I haven't brought her up or pursued her since. So I am not focused on her at all. My question to you, Leo, is: did you genuinely miss my second statement where I stepped back from Isha, or are you deliberately framing me as locked in a grudge to manufacture friction? Since this is my third and final speaking turn of Day 1, I also want to leave my position clear to everyone: all nine players have spoken, and no concrete, checkable evidence of mafia behavior has been produced. Forcing a blind elimination on Day 1 carries a heavy risk of losing a town member, so I do not support lynching on flimsy tone reads today. I'll be watching how everyone votes or abstains, as that record will be crucial tomorrow. Leo, I'd like you to answer for that mischaracterization.

Kenji, fair correction. I misread your position. You did step back from Isha in your sixth speech, and I should have acknowledged that instead of framing you as still locked on her. That was a sloppy premise on my part, not a deliberate distortion. Your answer also clarifies things for the table: you dropped the Isha float early and have not returned to it. Where I still differ is the tone of your last turn. You asked me to answer for a mischaracterization and framed it as a demand, which is a lot of heat for a Day 1 disagreement over wording. I'd rather we keep the pressure on evidence and behavior. My position is unchanged: no accusation and no vote today. The table can weigh how each of us handled this exchange, and I'll be watching the votes and abstentions as closely as you are.

Lucia here. The Kenji–Leo exchange is the only new concrete thing on the board: Leo misread Kenji's position, Kenji corrected him sharply, and Leo acknowledged the mistake rather than digging in. I don't think that exchange by itself justifies a vote against either of them. It shows Leo was sloppy, and it shows Kenji can apply heat, but neither is a checkable mafia tell. The more important point is that we still have zero concrete behavioral evidence against anyone, and multiple players have said they won't vote without it. I share that position: absent a specific, checkable claim, I would rather abstain than help force a weak elimination. The vote record matters, but a record of votes cast on nothing is not much better than abstentions, and it can hand mafia an easy miselimination. Zara, you emphasized the value of the vote record and the risk of manufacturing agreement. Given where the day stands, if no concrete case emerges before voting, will you abstain, or would you still cast a protest vote on a weak read? I ask because your answer will tell us whether you see the record itself as worth more than the risk of a bad lynch.

Lucia, if no meaningful case emerges, I expect to abstain rather than cast a protest vote simply to create a record. A weak vote is unlikely to eliminate anyone without five votes, but it can still be misread or help build momentum around a poor case.

I do think votes based on honest, specific suspicions can be informative even when they fall short of an elimination. For now, though, I don't have a suspicion strong enough to vote on. Leo's mischaracterization and correction are worth remembering, but I don't see them as a sufficient case by themselves.

Amara, second turn. Taking stock of where the day stands: all nine of us have spoken, multiple players have explicitly stated they won't vote without concrete evidence, and no concrete behavioral case has been put forward by anyone. The most substantive exchange remains the Leo-Kenji mischaracterization, which resolved itself cleanly but at least produced a moment worth remembering.

What I want to flag is the meta-position we're approaching. If the table collectively abstains, we lose a full day with no elimination and no vote record to parse — we reset to the same zero-evidence position on Day 2. If we force a vote on nothing, we risk handing mafia an easy miselimination. Neither is ideal, but they aren't equivalent: a day with no vote record gives us strictly less to work with than a day where we at least see how people's instincts and reasoning align, even if the vote falls short of five.

That said, I understand the hesitation. A vote cast on tone reads alone is noise, and noise can mislead as easily as silence.

Priya, you noted earlier that voting records are one of our few hard data points going into tomorrow. Given that no concrete case has emerged, do you think the collective absence of a vote record itself tells us something useful, or does it simply leave us exactly where we started — nine players, zero evidence, one day burned?

Amara, a unanimous abstention would tell us that nobody was willing to commit to a vote, but it would be hard to distinguish shared caution from mafia going along with the consensus. It isn't exactly a reset: we have today's statements, and a night may bring a death or private investigation result. But we shouldn't assume those will resolve anything either.

A reasoned vote can be informative even without an elimination or a revealed role; the reasons and reactions can be compared with later developments. Still, I don't think a vote made solely to fill the record is valuable enough to justify inventing a suspicion. At present, I don't have a case strong enough to vote on. Leo's misreading and correction are worth revisiting if a pattern develops, but aren't enough by themselves.

Maya, second turn. Let me respond to what's actually new and then put one question to one person. Priya's answer to Amara is the most useful thing anyone has said since my first turn, and it refines my own view rather than changing it. She points out that unanimous abstention and a reasoned-but-unsuccessful vote are not symmetric: a vote record gives us a comparison set for tomorrow, whereas silence gives us nothing but the statements we already have. Amara framed the choice as "no record" versus "a bad lynch." I want to refine that: those are not the only two options, and the third option is the one nobody has named — a split vote with concrete stated reasons that falls short of five. That outcome costs us no elimination, hands mafia nothing, and still produces the alignment data Amara wants. Leo's framing of the cost of a weak lynch is correct about permanent loss of a town voice, but it assumes the only alternative to a bad elimination is no lynch, and a dispersed vote record doesn't require anyone to hang a villager. So my position, stated plainly so it can't be misread: I do not support eliminating anyone today. I also don't support manufacturing a suspicion to fill a ballot. If someone has a concrete, checkable claim, I will vote for it and say exactly why. If nobody does by the time voting opens, I will consider a vote on the thinnest genuinely-held read rather than a unanimous abstention, purely because Priya and Amara are right that "nobody was willing to commit" is nearly indistinguishable from "the group agreed and nobody minded." That's a real asymmetry, and pretending otherwise costs us the one hard data point we have. One thing I want to correct about the framing Sam set up in his first turn, because it has been quoted back at me twice now and I don't think it survives scrutiny. Sam said that a mafioso manufacturing a name-drop usually comes with at least a thin veneer of justification, since the point is to make the target stick. That is a claim about what mafia usually do, and it was used to imply that Isha's lack of a veneer is exculpatory. I don't think it holds. A mafioso who labels their own read as baseless is not making the target stick — they are making the target memorable while making themselves look transparent. Transparency is cheap and costs nothing to perform, and I said as much in my first turn before I saw the pattern get treated as evidence in one direction only. The honest statement is that Isha's framing is compatible with both alignments, which is what Priya said, and I want to be clear that I was too quick to build a framework around a single exchange. That said, I don't want to throw the exchange away entirely, because there is one specific thing in it that is checkable and that nobody has examined. Isha said

Lucia, final turn. I still have no concrete, checkable case against anyone. The Kenji–Leo exchange was sloppy and then corrected; it is memorable but not enough to vote on. Isha’s early name-drop was explicitly disclaimed, which is compatible with either alignment, and Sam’s inference from it was too confident. I will not manufacture a suspicion to fill a ballot. If voting opens with no concrete claim, I expect to abstain, and I want my position clear: I am not accusing Kenji, Leo, Isha, Sam, Maya, Priya, Amara, or Zara. One loose end matters before votes: Maya’s last turn ended mid-sentence after “Isha said,” and she said there was one specific checkable thing nobody had examined. Maya, please finish that specific point: what exactly did Isha say that is checkable, and what should we compare it to? I am asking because if it is concrete, it matters before voting; if it is another tone read, we should label it as such. That is my only question.

Lucia, here is the specific point, and I'll state it as a checkable inconsistency rather than a tone read.

Isha's first speech contains two statements that can be checked against each other inside that same speech. She said it was "no information yet" and that she had "no strong read on anyone" — and in the same message she produced one specific name, Kenji, and said it "keeps coming to my mind." Those cannot both be fully accurate. If she genuinely had no read on anyone, the natural output is no name at all, or a name flagged as arbitrary — and she did flag it as arbitrary. But "keeps coming to my mind," in the present progressive, describes a recurring familiarity with that one specific name before any in-game information existed. That points to the name already being salient to her rather than randomly surfaced.

Why I think this is checkable rather than another tone read: the comparison is her own words against each other, and the question has a verifiable answer.

Isha, one specific question: before any player had spoken, what did you know about Kenji — his seat order, his role in the setup, anything else — that made his name recur for you, and how is that compatible with "no information yet"? If the honest answer is "nothing, it was genuinely arbitrary," then this closes and I am done with it. If the answer is "I had some prior familiarity with that name," that is still not a mafia tell — plenty of town players have priors — but then "no information yet" was not quite accurate, and the table should hear that from her rather than from me.

Second, to be precise about what I am not saying: I am not claiming Isha is mafia. Sam's inference that a mafioso must attach a thin veneer was too confident, and I said so. Isha's transparency was genuine and cheap; transparency costs nothing to perform. A name-drop with no support and no veneer is compatible with both alignments, and Priya had that right before I did.

My position is unchanged: I do not support eliminating anyone today, and I will not manufacture a suspicion to fill a ballot. If Isha's answer is honest, my read of her is "first-mover artifact" and nothing more, and I would rather the group spend the vote record on dispersed, honestly-reasoned votes than on this. If she answers with something concrete, that is when I will move.

Maya, direct answer to your question: nothing. I didn't know Kenji's seat order, his role, or anything about him before he spoke. "Keeps coming to my mind" was casual phrasing for the name I kept landing on while deciding what to break the ice with. I was scanning a list of eight names, deciding who to float, and Kenji's was the one my mind settled on — that's all the phrase meant. I should have said "the name I kept circling back to while deciding," which would have been more precise, but I don't think the distinction matters because you've already answered your own question: if I had prior familiarity, that's still not a mafia tell, and you said so yourself.

What I find more notable is the trajectory of this exchange. I floated a baseless name openly, Kenji asked me about it, I answered honestly, Kenji accepted the answer and explicitly told the table not to tunnel on it — and we are now on what feels like the fifth round of examining that same three-sentence float. Meanwhile, Sam's confident claim that a mafioso must attach a veneer, which Priya correctly identified as too strong, has been acknowledged as wrong but keeps being treated as if it were still standing.

I want to be clear about my position: I have no case against anyone, I have not accused anyone, and I don't plan to vote for a name without a specific checkable behavior behind it. If no concrete case emerges, I'd rather abstain than manufacture consensus. But I'd ask everyone — including myself — to weigh whether continued scrutiny of a disclaimed float is helping the town or just giving us something comfortable to focus on while the actual mafia sit quietly in the room.

Amara, third and final turn. Let me take stock of where the day stands and state my position clearly.

All nine players have spoken. We've examined the Isha-Kenji exchange from multiple angles, the Leo-Kenji mischaracterization resolved itself, and Maya surfaced one concrete checkable inconsistency that Isha answered directly. None of it adds up to a case strong enough to justify a five-vote elimination, and every player who has addressed the question has said essentially the same thing.

Maya's refinement of the options is the most useful framing we have going into voting: a unanimous abstention tells us nothing distinguishable from mafia coasting on consensus, while a split vote with stated reasons gives us a comparison set without risking a miselimination. Priya made this point, Amara echoed it, and I agree. The third option — dispersed votes with honestly-held, stated reasons that fall short of five — costs us nothing and preserves the record.

My position: I do not support eliminating anyone today. If concrete evidence emerges before voting, I will reassess. Absent that, I expect to cast a vote on the thinnest genuinely-held read rather than abstain, purely because the record matters and I would rather give the table something to compare against on Day 2 than hand mafia a silent consensus.

No accusations. No blame assigned. The day's information budget is spent, and I think the most honest thing any of us can say is that we don't know enough yet — and that saying so openly is better than pretending otherwise.

Priya, final turn. Isha's explanation is consistent with her earlier disclaimer; I don't see a meaningful contradiction in having a name come to mind without a strong read.

One caution about dispersed votes: ballots are secret and simultaneous, so nobody can guarantee they will stay dispersed. A vote based on a thin read can contribute to an elimination even if its voter didn't intend one. Still, an honestly reasoned vote could be useful to compare with later statements and votes.

I don't currently have a suspicion strong enough to vote on, so I expect to abstain. That isn't evidence that everyone else should abstain; please state your actual reasons if you do vote.
Voting begins.
The votes are revealed.
No player received the required votes. Nobody is eliminated.
Night begins.
Mafia target preferences are shared privately before the final kill vote.
Maya is not mafia.
Maya was eliminated.
Day 2 begins.

Lucia here. Day 2 has one hard fact: Maya was killed by mafia, so she was town. That makes the Day 1 vote record much sharper. Isha and Amara both voted Maya; Leo voted Kenji; everyone else abstained. I’m not treating abstention as scummy by itself, but the two votes on a now-confirmed town player need direct explanation. Isha’s vote stands out most to me because Maya’s final substantive push was a specific checkable question to Isha, Isha answered it, and then Isha voted Maya anyway. Now Maya is dead. Isha, why did you choose Maya over abstaining on Day 1, and what exactly in Maya’s answer or behavior did you judge vote-worthy enough to put her name on the board? I’m not locking a vote yet, but that is my main lead. Amara also owes an explanation for the same vote, and I want to compare it with Isha’s before deciding. I still have no concrete case against Leo beyond his Kenji vote, and I’m not accusing the abstainers merely for caution. My current focus is the Maya voters, especially Isha given the timing.

Lucia, I'll answer your question directly: I voted Maya because she spent her final substantive turn building a targeted case against me — the "keeps coming to my mind" inconsistency — which I had already answered honestly and which I judged to be a thin line of questioning rather than real evidence. Voting the person most actively pushing suspicion on you when you believe the push is unfounded is a reasonable town action, not a red flag.

Your accusation rests on circular reasoning: "you voted Maya, mafia killed Maya, therefore you're suspicious." If that logic held, anyone who voted the night's kill target would be guilty — but nobody can predict mafia's target in advance. The relevant question is whether my stated reason for the vote was consistent with what I said before voting, and it was: I told the table I'd consider a vote on my thinnest genuine read rather than abstain, and Maya's direct push against me was exactly that.

I'd also note that Amara voted Maya too under the same stated logic. If my vote warrants scrutiny, hers should be examined with equal rigor — I'd like to hear how she weighed her decision, since her reasoning process was similar to mine and comparing the two may tell us more than pressing one voter.

Amara here, addressing Lucia's direct request for an explanation of my Day 1 vote on Maya.

My reasoning was transparent at the time: I had already stated publicly that I expected to cast a vote on the thinnest genuinely-held read rather than abstain, because the record matters. My thinnest read at the time was Maya — she was the most active player building frameworks around single exchanges, and her last turn cut off mid-sentence while building a specific case against Isha. That discontinuity wasn't a mafia tell, but it was the most distinctive behavior on the board when I cast my vote.

Isha's point deserves weight: the accusation that "you voted the night's kill target, therefore you're suspicious" is circular. Nobody chooses mafia's target. If that logic held, any random vote becomes incriminating whenever the target dies. What matters is whether the stated reason was consistent with prior positions, and mine was — I said I'd vote on a thin read, and I did, and I said why.

That said, I want to be honest about the uncomfortable fact: both players who voted Maya are now the two names Lucia has flagged. That's not nothing, and I won't pretend it away. If the table wants to scrutinize both Maya voters equally, I welcome that. Isha should answer your question fully and I already have. Comparing our reasoning side by side is exactly the right move — and if either of our answers doesn't hold up to scrutiny, the table will see it.

My current position: I still have no concrete case against anyone. The most useful thing now is to hear from the players who abstained about what, if anything, could change their minds about voting today. Leo, you voted Kenji — what specific behavior drove that vote, and does the Maya kill change your read on anyone?

Amara, you asked directly, so here is my answer. My vote on Kenji was not random. Kenji challenged Isha twice, and when I misread his position he demanded that I answer for it and treated a Day 1 disagreement as something that needed an apology. I said I would only vote on specific, checkable behavior, and the heat he applied in that exchange is the closest thing I had. That is a thin read, and I admit it falls short of the standard I set for myself. Maya's death does not change my read on Kenji, because Maya being town tells us nothing about Kenji's alignment. It does sharpen what Lucia is asking. The two Maya votes need explanation, and I agree with Amara that they should be compared side by side rather than judged in isolation. Lucia, you said your only concrete concern with me is my Kenji vote. I accept that, and I'll keep it open to scrutiny. Maya's last substantive turn was a question about Isha's first speech, and Isha answered it directly. A vote on Maya after that answer may have been reasonable, but it is exactly the kind of vote we should examine rather than defend by default. Kenji, my question to you: on Day 1 you said you had dropped the Isha float and would not return to it, yet your later messages kept pressing me and Isha. What would you need to see from a player to stop escalating a dispute? And does Maya's death change how you view the votes cast on her?

Leo, to answer your first question: you are once again misrepresenting my record. After speech 6, I never pressed Isha again. In speech 15, I was solely responding to you because you falsely claimed I was still focused on her. What stops an escalating dispute is simple: accurate representation of what was said. When a player repeatedly invents a narrative that I am tunneling or pressing someone when the transcript plainly shows I stepped back, I will correct it.

Now, regarding your second question and how Maya's death affects my view of the votes: Maya being night-killed confirms she was a villager. The votes cast by Isha and Amara against Maya certainly deserve close scrutiny, especially given that Maya was actively pressing Isha right before the vote. rules:
1. Players and roles

9 players: 2 mafia, 1 police/detective, 1 doctor, 5 villagers.
Mafia know each other. Only players who are still alive can act.

2. Team victory

Town wins when all mafia are eliminated. Mafia win when their count equals or exceeds the town count.
There is no day limit. Play continues until town or mafia wins.
A request budget can pause play without declaring a winner.

3. Day discussion and votes

Each day starts with discussion. Players then submit secret votes at the same time. A day vote may target any living player, including the voter.
Players may abstain. All votes and abstentions are revealed together. Everyone sees exactly who voted for whom.
The full named voting history remains available on later turns.
The unique leader is eliminated only if they receive at least half the living players' votes, rounded up. If the highest vote count is tied, nobody is eliminated.

4. Mafia preferences

At night, when more than one mafia survives, each privately points once to a living town player.
Each mafia chooses without seeing the other current choices.
The choices are shared with surviving mafia only after all mafia have pointed.
These preferences are nonbinding. They do not decide the final kill vote.
A single surviving mafia skips this step and votes directly.

5. Final night vote

After the preferences are shared, each mafia submits a secret vote to kill one living town player.
The mafia submit their final votes at the same time.
The target with the most votes is selected. A seeded random choice breaks a tie for the highest count.
Resolve this vote and any tie before checking doctor protection.

6. Police investigations

Each police/detective checks one other living player each night.
Only that police player gets the result: mafia or not mafia.
The result does not give the exact town role.
Each police player acts independently. Police and doctors do not know each other's identities.

7. Doctor protection

Each doctor secretly protects one living player each night, including themselves.
The doctor can protect the same player on consecutive nights.
If the mafia target is protected by any doctor, nobody dies.
Protection lasts for that night only. Each doctor acts independently.
Doctors remember their own choices. They receive no private confirmation of an attack.

8. Night resolution

All night actions resolve simultaneously, including actions submitted by a player killed that night.
The public hears only who died or that nobody died.

9. Information and limits

Roles are not revealed when a player dies or is eliminated.
Public announcements identify only who was eliminated, never their role.
There are no further powers, free-form private chat, or tools.
